issues.description: The problem statement and solution expect Stock.findStockIngredient(String) but the template's Stock class defines findStockIngredient(String, boolean). This parameter mismatch causes calls to findStockIngredient(ingredient) in the template (and the usage in the problem examples) to not match any method signature, leading to compilation errors and confusion about which method students should implement.
issues.suggestedFix: Change the template Stock class to provide findStockIngredient(String name) (matching the UML and solution). Either rename the existing method to remove the boolean parameter or add an overloaded findStockIngredient(String) that delegates to the boolean version (e.g., treating case sensitivity as appropriate). Ensure all calls in the template and examples match this signature so students can compile and follow the specification.

issues.description: The problem statement and solution define Stock.findStockIngredient(String) (single-argument) but the template Stock class provides findStockIngredient(String, boolean) (two-argument). This mismatch of method signature for the same conceptual operation (finding a stock ingredient by name) creates a mapping and compilation confusion: students reading the spec expect a single-argument method, the tests and solution use it, yet the starter code only exposes a different signature. Students may be unable to call the intended method or will have to discover the differing signature, adding unnecessary cognitive load.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the template Stock API with the problem statement and solution by adding or replacing the method with the single-argument signature: public StockIngredient findStockIngredient(String name). If case-sensitivity control is desired, provide an overloaded method or internal parameter (e.g., keep findStockIngredient(String name, boolean caseSensitive) and add public StockIngredient findStockIngredient(String name) that delegates to it) so students and tests can use the specified single-argument version.
